newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany accuses Libya of "terrorist" bomb attack.
newsitem.headline: Germany accuses Libya of "terrorist" bomb attack.

text.p: German prosecutors on Friday blamed Libya for a 1986 bomb attack on a West Berlin nightclub which provoked a U.S. air strike on Tripoli that killed the adopted infant daughter of leader Muammar Gaddafi.

State prosecutor Dieter Neumann said five people had been charged after prosecutors had found evidence Libya planned the attack against the United States in retaliation for the sinking of a Libyan ship shortly before the bombing.
"The Libyan secret service issued an order on March 26 (1986) to use a terrorist act to strike at an American object in Berlin as a reaction to that," Neumann said.
Two U.S. soldiers and a Turkish woman were killed and scores of off-duty U.S. military personnel were wounded when the bomb exploded in the middle of the crowded La Belle nightclub.

Washington immediately blamed Libya for the blast in Berlin's Schoeneberg district and bombed the Arab state, killing at least 15 people including Gaddafi's adopted daughter, and wounding more than 100.

Neumann said prosecutors had charged five people with the attack, including a former member of the Libyan secret service, Musbah Eter, and a Palastinian, Yasser Shraydi. They were both at the Libyan embassy in East Berlin at the time.
They also charged three German nationals, named as Verena Chanaa, her former husband Ali Chanaa and her sister Andrea Haeussler.
Shraydi, along with the Chanaas, was charged with three counts of murder and setting the explosion. The others were charged with aiding and abetting the crime.
Neumann said all the accused were in custody apart from Eter, who he said had made a confession to prosecutors that helped them to solve the case.

In an odd twist, Neumann said investigators had found evidence in files of the former East German security police (Stasi) that they had taken steps to prevent the attack on the nightclub, but their efforts were blocked by the East German government.
"It was a strange situation in which the security police actually took steps, in certain areas, to prevent this attack," Neumann said. "The East German government apparently blocked this."
The target of the attack, and who was to carry it out, were only decided shortly before the bombing, he said.
Chanaa had spied on the Libyan embassy for the Stasi and therefore had to do something in return for Libya, said state prosecutor Detlev Mehlis, investigating the case since 1986.

Mehlis said the Chanaa couple built the bomb containing three kgs (six pounds) of plastic explosive in their apartment, and then Verena Chanaa and her sister Hauessler drove to the disco and planted the bomb near the dance floor.
